reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in education is modest and has recently fallen. Per the Census Bureau, 30.0% of firms in Educational services (NAICS 61) answered Yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, down from 35.5% in the prior period. The series was first asked in September 2023. That is the only hard adoption number the material offers, and it describes firms in the sector rather than classrooms or institutions specifically.

What the deployments look like comes mainly from the federal government. The Department of Education issued AI guidance for schools that frames permissible use, risk, and procurement, and it maintains an inventory of its own AI use-cases. Those use-cases are concrete and mostly administrative: CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly for written communication; Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration; and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. Other listed uses include generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in various programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, writing R code for data analysis, training employees on prompt engineering, automating conversion between data types such as a county name to its FIPS code, generating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, researching public articles and policies, testing filters against fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information, and suggesting descriptive paragraphs, workflow diagrams, and qualifications for public positions. The emphasis is on drafting, summarization, transcription, and internal operations rather than instruction.

Where money and attention concentrate is tracked by HolonIQ, which describes itself as a platform for impact market intelligence covering the global impact economy, including sizing addressable markets, forecasting demand, quantifying impact with rubrics and ratings, mapping partners and competitors, and serving governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms, and investors. Its page states that the global media relies on it for insight and data on the global impact economy. The curated points describe HolonIQ as covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. The excerpts do not report specific funding totals or adoption rates for education, so no figures can be cited here.

The workforce and skills side is covered by this site's own course catalog. It lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each, re-verified daily. The catalog names DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, DeepLearning.AI with Stanford, Google, Hugging Face, and Andrej Karpathy, alongside university graduate courses: Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191. It notes that four are university graduate courses with public materials while the rest come from industry, that university courses tend to be structured around exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, and that only three list an accompanying public code repository. The catalog explicitly does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

On risk and regulation, the material is thin. The Department of Education's guidance is the only regulatory posture described, and it is framed around adherence to federal regulations, responsible and secure usage, and innovation under an executive order on American leadership in AI. The page mentions data loss prevention and filters for prohibited prompt information among the Department's own use-cases. The excerpts do not describe enforcement, penalties, or state-level rules for education.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few cautious takeaways. Adoption among education firms sits at 30.0% per the Census Bureau, so this is not yet a majority practice. The documented federal use-cases cluster in back-office and communication tasks, which is where the clearest examples of value appear. The course catalog suggests the skills pipeline spans free industry material and university coursework, with the choice between them a matter of learning style rather than rigor. Beyond that, the sources are largely silent on ROI evidence, vendor spending, and specific compliance obligations, and nothing here should be read as filling those gaps.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
